# Acids, Bases and Salts

## Core ideas and reasoning

Salts form when acid hydrogen is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. Select preparation by solubility and reactivity. To make a soluble salt from an insoluble base or carbonate, add excess solid to warm dilute acid, filter off excess and crystallise the filtrate. Excess ensures the acid is used up. To prepare a soluble sodium, potassium or ammonium salt from an alkali, use titration to find neutralising volumes, then repeat without indicator before crystallising. An insoluble salt can be made by precipitation from two soluble solutions, followed by filtration, washing and drying. Do not attempt to filter a dissolved salt out of solution. Carbonates react with acids to form salt, water and carbon dioxide; oxides and hydroxides form salt and water. Include states in ionic equations and cancel spectator ions. Hydrated salts incorporate water in their crystals; heating may remove it, but strong heating can also decompose the salt.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Describe preparing copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

Add excess CuO to warm dilute acid with stirring, filter unreacted oxide, gently concentrate the blue filtrate, cool to crystallise, then separate and dry crystals.

### Example 2

Write the ionic equation for precipitating silver chloride.

Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s). The white precipitate forms when suitable soluble solutions are mixed.

### Example 3

Why is titration used when preparing sodium chloride from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide?

Both reactants are soluble, so excess cannot be filtered off. Titration determines neutralising volumes; repeat without indicator to obtain an uncontaminated salt solution.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
